In this notebook we look at two metrics for determining whether or not two metaprograms generated from different sample groups are shared. 
The overall goal is to identify a strategy for counting how many metaprograms in the full cohort of SKC samples are found in a specific subset. 

Here we look at 4 different subsets: 

- `subset_001`: 10 samples
- `subset_002`: 10 samples
- `subset_006`: 20 samples
- `subset_007`: 20 samples 

For each metaprogram in a given subset we compare it to all metaprograms in the full cohort and calculate: 

- The correlation of gene weights
- The Jaccard index between the top 200 genes

## Define functions 

```{r shared-functions}
# helper function to get all possible pairs for two lists
# uses the names of each list to get the pairs 
# expects a list of metaprograms where names are the names of the metaprograms
get_pairs <- function(list1, list2){
  
  # get all possible mp pairs
  pairs_df <- expand.grid(
    subset_mp = names(list1),
    full_mp = names(list2),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
}

# calculate significance for permutation testing
# reports a pvalue for a specified statistic 
calculate_permutation_significance <- function(
    stat, 
    observed_df, 
    background_df, 
    join_columns, 
    nreps
){
  
  # combine the observed values with the background
  combined_df <- observed_df |> 
    dplyr::select(
      subset_mp,
      full_mp,
      obs_value = {{ stat }}
    ) |> 
    dplyr::left_join(background_df, by = join_columns) |> 
    dplyr::select(-replicate)
  
  # calculate the pvalue for num genesets 
  pvalue_df <- combined_df |> 
    dplyr::mutate(
      # indicate which rows have background > obs
      greater_than_obs = {{ stat }} >= obs_value
    ) |> 
    dplyr::summarize(
      # calculate p values and retain a column with the observed value
      obs_value = unique(obs_value),
      pvalue = (sum(greater_than_obs) +1)/(nreps + 1),
      .by = c("subset_mp", "full_mp")
    ) |> 
    # add adjusted pvalue 
    dplyr::mutate(
      adj_pvalue = p.adjust(pvalue, method = "BH"),
      is_significant = adj_pvalue <= 0.05
    )
  
  return(pvalue_df)
  
}
```


```{r correlation-functions}

# function to shuffle mp1 and calculate the correlation with mp2
# each vector is a vector of gene weights and named with gene ids
permute_metaprogram_correlation <- function(mp1, mp2, nreps = 1000) {
  
  # only consider genes that are in both
  genes <- union(names(mp1), names(mp2))
  
  # make sure the order is the same
  mp1 <- mp1[genes]
  mp2 <- mp2[genes]
  
  replicate(
    nreps,
    # shuffle the gene weights and calculate the correlation
    cor(sample(mp1), mp2, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  )
}

# for each subset, compare each metaprogram to every metaprogram in the full cohort
# to get the observed calculation 
# for all metaprograms in the subset, shuffle the gene weights and recalculate 
# correlation to get a background distribution
# calculate p value for each comparison
metaprogram_correlation_test <- function(mps_subset, mps_full, nreps = 1000){
  
  # get all possible paris of subset and full cohort mps
  pairs_df <- get_pairs(mps_subset, mps_full)
  
  # calculate the correlation for all possible pairs of metaprograms
  obs_df <- pairs_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      correlation = purrr::map2_dbl(
        subset_mp, full_mp,
        \(x, y) {
          
          # get the actual metaprograms from the names stored in pairs_df
          subset <- mps_subset[[x]]
          full <- mps_full[[y]]
          
          # make sure metaprograms are in the right order and then calculate correlation
          genes <- union(names(subset), names(full))
          subset <- subset[genes]
          full <- full[genes]
          cor(subset, full, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
          
        }
      )
    )
  
  # get a background distribution for each combination of metaprograms 
  background_df <- pairs_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      background_correlation = purrr::map2(
        subset_mp, full_mp,
        # shufle the subset mp and calculate correlation with full mp
        \(x, y) permute_metaprogram_correlation(
          mps_subset[[x]], 
          mps_full[[y]],
          nreps = nreps
        )
      )
    ) |>
    # get one row per replicate
    tidyr::unnest_longer(background_correlation, values_to = "correlation", indices_to = "replicate")
  
  # calculate the pvalue for each combination
  pvalue_df <- calculate_permutation_significance(
    correlation, 
    obs_df, 
    background_df, 
    join_columns = c("subset_mp", "full_mp"),
    nreps
    ) |>
    dplyr::rename(correlation = obs_value) 
  
  return(list("pvalue" = pvalue_df, "background" = background_df))
  
}
```

```{r jaccard-functions}
# helper function for getting the jaccard index between two vectors
calc_jaccard <- function(vec1, vec2){
  jaccard <- length(intersect(vec1, vec2)) / length(union(vec1, vec2))
  return(jaccard)
}

# create a background distribution for jaccard index
# grab random subsets of genes from the gene universe and calculate the overlap 
# with the top 200 genes from each of the full mps 
permute_jaccard <- function(subset_gene_universe, full_top_genes, nreps){
  
  background <- replicate(
    nreps, {
      
      # get 200 genes randomly from the subset gene universe
      subset_genes <- sample(subset_gene_universe, 200)
      
      # for each full mp calculate the jaccard between the random gene set
      # and the top 200 genes for the full mp
      full_top_genes |> 
        purrr::imap(\(full_genes, mp){
          
          data.frame(
            full_mp = mp,
            jaccard = calc_jaccard(subset_genes, full_genes)
          )
        }) |> 
        dplyr::bind_rows()
    },
    simplify = FALSE
  ) |> 
    dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "replicate")
  
  return(background)
  
}

# here we calculate the overlap in the top 200 genes from the subset mp and the full mp 
# to get a background distribution we randomly select 200 genes from the subset gene universe
# and get the Jaccard between that random gene set and the observed full metaprogram 
# we then calculate the empirical pvalue for each subset metaprogram compared to each full metaprogram
top_genes_test <- function(subset_top_genes, subset_gene_universe, full_top_genes, nreps = 1000){
  
  # get all possible pairs of subset and full cohort mps
  pairs_df <- get_pairs(subset_top_genes, full_top_genes)
  
  # get the obersved jaccard index for overlap of all possible combinations
  obs_df <- pairs_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      jaccard = purrr::map2_dbl(
        subset_mp, full_mp,
        \(x, y) {
          
          subset <- subset_top_genes[[x]]
          full <- full_top_genes[[y]]
          
          calc_jaccard(subset, full)
          
        }
      )
    )
  
  # generate a background distribution 
  # only one per subset being tested
  background_df <- permute_jaccard(subset_gene_universe, full_top_genes, nreps)
  
  # get the pvalue for each combination of subset and full mp
  pvalue_df <- calculate_permutation_significance(
    jaccard, 
    obs_df, 
    background_df, 
    "full_mp", 
    nreps
  ) |>
    dplyr::rename(jaccard = obs_value) 
  
  return(list("pvalue" = pvalue_df, "background" = background_df))
  
}
```

```{r plotting-functions}
# helper function for plotting permutation results
# plots background points with observed values in color on top as sina plot

# for each subset make a faceted plot where the facets are the metaprograms in the full cohort 
# the x axis is the metaprogram in the subset
# the y axis is the correlation where both background and observed are shown 
# color by significant or not significant 
plot_permutation_results <- function(pvalue_df, background_df, x_axis, stat, subset_id){
  
  ggplot(background_df, aes(x = {{ x_axis }}, y = {{ stat }})) +
    ggforce::geom_sina(
      color = "gray",
      alpha = 0.1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = pvalue_df,
      aes(
        x = {{ x_axis }},
        y = {{ stat }},
        color = is_significant
      ),
      size  = 3,
      shape = 18  # diamond
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "red", `FALSE` = "blue")) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = subset_id
    )
  
}

# make a heatmap with metaprograms from the full cohort on the x axis
# metaprograms from the subset as rows and colored by a statistic (either correlation or jaccard)
# significant observations are showmn with *
plot_stat_heatmap <- function(pvalue_df, subset_id, stat){
  
  # create the matrix with the values for the specified stat
  stat_mat <- pvalue_df |>
    dplyr::select(full_mp, subset_mp, all_of(stat)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = full_mp, values_from = all_of(stat)) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames("subset_mp") |>
    as.matrix()
  
  # get a matrix with significant text to overlap 
  sig_mat <- pvalue_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(label = dplyr::if_else(adj_pvalue <= 0.05, "*", "")) |>
    dplyr::select(full_mp, subset_mp, label) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = full_mp, values_from = label) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames("subset_mp") |>
    as.matrix()
  
  # make sure the significance levels are in the right order
  sig_mat <- sig_mat[rownames(stat_mat), colnames(stat_mat)]
  
  # build the heatmap
  heatmap <- ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
    stat_mat,
    name = stat,
    col  = circlize::colorRamp2(
      c(0, max(stat_mat, na.rm = TRUE)),
      c("white", "#B2182B")
    ),
    cell_fun = function(j, i, x, y, width, height, fill) {
      if (sig_mat[i, j] == "*")
        grid::grid.text("*", x, y, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 14, col = "black"))
    },
    column_title = "Full cohort metaprogram",
    row_title  = "Subset metaprogram",
    column_title_side = "bottom",
    cluster_rows  = FALSE,
    cluster_columns = FALSE,
    row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10),
    column_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10),
    border = TRUE
  )
  
  # add an overall title with the subset id
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(
    heatmap,
    column_title    = subset_id,
    column_title_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold")
  )
}

```



## Correlation of gene weights

First we will calculate the correlation of all gene weights using Pearson correlation with pairwise complete observations. 
To determine if the correlation is significantly greater than random chance, we will shuffle the gene weights for the subset metaprogram and re-calculate the correlation to each full metaprogram to create a null distribution. 
This will be used to calculate an empirical pvalue. 


```{r}
# extract the metaprogram list from each object
# this is a list of all metaprograms with a vector of gene weights
all_subset_mps <- subset_mp_list |> 
  purrr::map("metaprogram_list")

# extract the full metaprogram list
full_mps <- full_cohort_mp_list$metaprogram_list

# calculate the correlation and test significance
# returns a list of pvalue_df, background_df for each subset id
all_correlation_list <- all_subset_mps |> 
  purrr::map(\(subset_mps) metaprogram_correlation_test(subset_mps, full_mps))
```

The below plot shows the correlation of each subset metaprogram with each full metaprogram. 
Each facet is a full metaprogram and the x axis of each plot is a subset metaprogram. 
The grey dots indicate the background distribution and colored diamonds indicate the observed values. 

```{r}
#| fig.height: 7
#| fig.width: 7

# plot the background and observed values for each metaprogram combination 
# facets are the metaprograms in the full cohort and then each metaprogram in the subset 
# is shown on the x axis 
all_correlation_list |> 
  purrr::iwalk(\(results_list, id){
    plot <- plot_permutation_results(
      results_list$pvalue,
      results_list$background,
      subset_mp,
      correlation,
      id
    ) + facet_wrap(vars(full_mp)) 
    
    print(plot)
  })
```

This heatmap shows the observed correlation between the full metaprograms (columns) and the subset metaprogram (rows).
The presence of * indicates the correlation is statistically significantly greater than random chance. 

```{r}
# make a heatmap where we color by correlation and label significant mps
all_correlation_list |> 
  purrr::map("pvalue") |> 
  purrr::iwalk(\(df, id) plot_stat_heatmap(df, id, "correlation"))
```

In looking at this we see that pretty much all correlations > 0 are considered significant based on the background distribution. 
This seems like we might be over estimating the amount of shared metaprograms, as I don't think we want to consider metaprograms with a correlation of 0.1 as shared. 
We might want to think about using a cutoff instead of permutation testing here, like 0.5. 

## Overlap of top 200 genes 

Here we look at the overlap of the top 200 genes for each metaprogram using the Jaccard similarity index. 
We calculate the observed Jaccard similarity index between each pair of subset and full metaprograms and compare that to a background distribution to see if the overlap is greater than random chance. 
For each subset, we take the full gene set universe and grab random sets of 200 genes. 
We then calculate the Jaccard index of that random set of genes with every metaprogram in the full cohort to get our background distribution.


```{r}
# extract the top 200 genes for each of the full cohort mps
full_top_genes <- full_cohort_metrics_list$top_genes

# get a list of gene universe for each subset
subset_gene_universe_list <- subset_mp_list |> 
  purrr::map("gene_universe")

# top genes for each metaprogram for each subset
all_subset_top_genes <- subset_metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map("top_genes")
```


```{r}
#| warning: FALSE 

# note this causes a warning because each full mp has multiple matches for every pair with subset mp
# test for jaccard index significance for each metaprogram within each subset
jaccard_pvalue_df_list <- purrr::map2(
  all_subset_top_genes,
  subset_gene_universe_list,
  \(top_genes, universe){
    top_genes_test(top_genes, universe, full_top_genes)
  }
)
```

Since we are using the full gene set universe for each subset to construct the background, we will only have one background per full metaprogram for each subset ID rather than for each combination of subset metaprograms and full metaprograms. 
We only show the full metaprogram on the x axis below and then each diamond indicates the observed value for a single metaprogram in the subset. 

```{r}
jaccard_pvalue_df_list |> 
  purrr::iwalk(\(results_list, id){
    plot <- plot_permutation_results(
      results_list$pvalue,
      results_list$background,
      full_mp,
      jaccard,
      id
    ) |> 
      print()
  })
```

The heatmap below shows only the observed values with the full metaprograms in columns and subset metaprograms in rows. 
The * indicates the Jaccard index is significantly greater than random chance. 


```{r}
# heatmap looking at jaccard between every metaprogram in subset and full 
# text indicates significant overlaps 
jaccard_pvalue_df_list |> 
  purrr::map("pvalue") |> 
  purrr::iwalk(\(df, id) plot_stat_heatmap(df, id, "jaccard"))
```

Overall we see fewer significant overlaps than with correlation and we see values that are more consistent with what 
I would expect to be a "significant" overlap. 
But we do still see occasional significance for Jaccard indices less than 0.1, which seems like very minimal overlap. 
I'm not sure I would want to call that "shared" so perhaps we also need a cutoff here? 


## Combine metrics

Ultimately we only want to keep metaprograms that are significant in both correlation and overlap. 
For each subset, we want to count how many of the full metaprograms are recapitulated based on passing these criteria. 

### Significance

First we will count how many of the full metaprograms have at least one metaprogram in each subset that is significant for both correlation and Jaccard. 

```{r}
# combine all pvalue dfs from all subsets for correlation
all_cor_df <- all_correlation_list |> 
  purrr::map("pvalue") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "subset_id") |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    cor_pvalue = pvalue,
    cor_adj_pvalue = adj_pvalue,
    cor_is_significant = is_significant
  )

# combine all pvalue dfs from all subsets for jaccard
all_jaccard_df <- jaccard_pvalue_df_list |> 
  purrr::map("pvalue") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "subset_id") |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    jaccard_pvalue = pvalue,
    jaccard_adj_pvalue = adj_pvalue,
    jaccard_is_significant = is_significant
  )

# put everything together for filtering and counting
all_results_df <- all_cor_df |> 
  dplyr::left_join(all_jaccard_df, by = c("subset_id", "subset_mp", "full_mp"))
```

```{r}
all_results_df |> 
  # for each mp combo, is it shared? 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_shared = cor_is_significant & jaccard_is_significant
  ) |> 
  # for each full mp in each subset is at least 1 mp shared? 
  dplyr::summarize(
    is_shared = any(is_shared),
    .by = c("full_mp", "subset_id")
  ) |> 
  # count the total shared metaprograms for each subset
  dplyr::summarize(
    total_shared = sum(is_shared),
    .by = c("subset_id")
  )
```

Using this approach, we return all 7 metaprograms for 3 out of 4 subsets. 
Although this may be real, I don't love allowing such low correlations and low Jaccard indices to be considered as "shared". 

### Cutoff 

As an alternative approach, we could define a minimum cutoff for each metric. 
Here we could set a minimum and combine it with permutation testing, requiring metaprograms to be significant and meet a minimum threshold. 

First, let's just look at the distribution of the observed correlation and Jaccard value for all possible pairs. 
We can use this to define a cutoff for each value. 

```{r}
ggplot(all_cor_df, aes(x = subset_id, y = correlation)) + 
  geom_boxplot()

ggplot(all_jaccard_df, aes(x = subset_id, y = jaccard)) + 
  geom_boxplot()
```

For correlation, I think saying anything above 0.5 is reasonable. 
This is also consistent with how we measure correlation of metaprograms within a cohort in our original metrics. 

For Jaccard, the values tend to be lower and closer to 0. 
If we follow the same logic as correlation and pick something right around where the tail of the distribution starts, we might want to use something like 0.2. 
Although, I feel like if we really want to be stringent we could increase that up to 0.5. 

Let's see how many metaprograms are shared if we use a correlation cutoff of 0.5 and Jaccard cutoff of 0.2.

```{r}
all_results_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_shared = cor_is_significant & jaccard_is_significant & correlation >= 0.5 & jaccard >= 0.2
  ) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    is_shared = any(is_shared),
    .by = c("full_mp", "subset_id")
  ) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    total_shared = sum(is_shared),
    .by = c("subset_id")
  )
```

Now we see that `subset_007` only shares 6 metaprograms instead of all 7. 
Note that moving the cutoff up to 0.5 for Jaccard results in 3-4 shared metaprograms per subset.
